title: The Empty Cloth Negotiations
summary: Public mural art and independent reporting expose conflicts of interest during a long slump, while an unmarked cloth gains contested meanings at negotiations.
history: After several seasons of falling prices in 1123, Talassar merchants reduced wages while their stored obligations retained old values. A mural painter simplified laboring figures into bright curved forms visible across crowded quays. A public reader investigated a councilor’s splendid house and found that its builder also received favorable canal contracts. The reader lost her sponsored platform but continued recitations in market yards. Negotiators began carrying plain cloth to request safe passage, although some courts treated the sign as surrender and others as a request to speak. Confusion allowed creditors to seize people approaching in good faith. Shared standards emerged slowly from recorded incidents rather than a single heroic proclamation.
question: how negotiated access and old debts can be revised while households still need the contracts maintaining their canals.
transformations: A painter’s simplified, accessible treatment of working subjects becomes large quay murals suited to crowded public space.
Investigative reporting on official conflicts of interest and loss of a sponsored platform become independent market recitation.
A prolonged slump with disputed measures becomes declining prices that coexist with unchanged hereditary assessments.
A protective negotiation sign with risks of misuse becomes plain cloth whose meaning requires explicit local agreement.
rows: Leven of the Curved Workers

Leven’s murals use simple forms so viewers across the quay can recognize load-bearing postures. Patrons call the workers interchangeable. She adds tool marks specific to each trade, insisting that public clarity need not erase the skill of the people represented.
The Reader’s Unsponsored Yard

After losing her covered platform, a reader continued beside a cooper’s yard. Rain damaged copies and reduced audiences. Neighbors supplied roofing without editorial control, creating a smaller but more dependable support than the official sponsorship she had lost.
The Falling Price Houses

These counting houses insist lower commodity prices prove prosperity, although workers’ fixed debts now consume larger shares of income. Their account books support both observations. The conflict concerns distribution and old obligations, not merely whether one broad description of the period is correct.
The House Contract Disclosure

A reader linked the councilor’s home repairs to canal awards through matching wood marks and delivery dates. Officials challenged her tone instead of the records. Later inquiry confirmed favorable treatment but left the councilor’s descendants occupying the improved house.
The First Empty Cloth

The cloth carries no heraldic mark and began as a request for conversation. One court filed it as submission. The claimant’s surviving petition specifies safe approach without concession, preserving a distinction that would determine whether later negotiators could risk entering the gate.
The Sign Explained Aloud

Negotiators state the cloth’s intended meaning before crossing a boundary. The receiving guard repeats it before witnesses. This cumbersome custom prevents assumptions becoming convenient evidence and makes safe approach depend upon a recorded exchange rather than a universally understood symbol.
The Price of the Same Basket

This comparison follows one basket of food, one week’s earnings, and one inherited payment over twenty seasons. Its narrow measures challenge sweeping claims of abundance or collapse. Households use it to propose actual adjustments rather than quarrel over the period’s name.
The Quay Paint Crab

Tiny crabs scrape mineral pigment spilled below mural walls. Their shells change hue temporarily. Festival sellers display them as living ancestral signatures, prompting the painter to demand cleaner work practices instead of treating contaminated animals as attractive proof of inspiration.
The Plain Cloth Landing

This landing admits recognized negotiators without charging a creditor’s toll. It remains outside the debt courts’ preferred approach. Porters maintain it through small contributions, giving distressed households a physical route to talks the formal system claims to welcome.
The Approach Without Submission

The rule separates requesting conversation from accepting judgment. Guards must record the visitor’s purpose. Creditors oppose it because it limits seizures at the gate, revealing how a supposedly neutral misunderstanding had supplied them with a profitable advantage.
Cera of the Contract Marks

Cera reads suppliers’ tool marks and compares work orders before publishing accusations. Her father repaired council buildings, making the inquiry personally awkward. She records his participation precisely, refusing either to hide it or turn a whole family history into a simple accusation.
The Councilor’s Bright House

The house is genuinely well built and still shelters several dependent relatives. Its improvement came through preferential contracts. Restitution proposals must distinguish returning illicit benefit from damaging a useful building or punishing occupants whose role in the transaction differed.
The Market Comparison Readers

Readers present prices alongside wages, rents, and quantities actually available. Sponsors prefer a single reassuring figure. The group keeps its measures public, allowing opponents to challenge the calculation without buying the platform from which the conclusion is announced.
The Cloth Gate Seizures

Several debtors were seized while carrying negotiation cloths. Guards recorded no arms but entered submission on the rolls. Correcting those records released some heirs from added fees, showing that an administrative description can continue a wrong long after the immediate capture.
The Mural’s Repair Patch

A repaired section uses cheaper pigment after sponsorship ended. Viewers initially called it artistic decline. The patch records the painter’s changed resources and the neighborhood’s continued work, making variation evidence of survival rather than a defect to conceal.
The Public Contract Supper

Officials attending must explain one maintenance contract before eating. Some refuse the invitation as disrespectful. Contractors who accept discover questions about supplies and labor that their formal tenders never ask, widening oversight beyond literate patrons.
The Dismissed Reader’s Copies

Independent copies preserve corrections beside the initial report. Hostile readers quote only corrected mistakes. Supporters sometimes remove the corrections. Cera insists they remain visible, because a dependable account must show how it changed when better evidence arrived.
The Cloth That Stays Wet

One negotiation cloth remains damp after a debtor’s release despite dry storage. Its fibers contain unusual salt, which explains part of the effect. Custodians also find an unresolved undertaking to provide shelter, leaving a finite claim still requiring action.
Contract Timber Marking

Suppliers mark beams before delivery and retain matching cut-offs. Those ordinary practices enabled the house investigation. New officials seek standardized royal stamps, while craftsmen argue that independent marks provide evidence precisely because no one authority controls every copy.
The Old Debt Price Review

Workers seek payments measured against current food costs. Creditors invoke authentic old undertakings. The hearing considers finite substitutions and compensated releases, requiring more practical work than declaring either inheritance sacred or every old promise meaningless.
